To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ability of hearing-impaired listeners to discriminate between highly similar harmonic complexes is significantly reduced compared with normal-hearing listeners.
the discrimination of spectral contrast by listeners with hearing impairment was significantly poorer than that for normal-hearing listeners.

listeners with hearing impairment require a larger amplitude difference between spectral peak and background harmonies to discriminate the peak location, compared to listeners with normal hearing, especially for spectral peaks located in higher frequency regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of hearing impairment on the ability of listeners to discriminate spectral contrast.
the ability of listeners to discriminate the spectral shape of harmonic complexes, a process that is critical to accurate perception of speech.
how the auditory system represents the frequency spectrum of complex sounds and the effects of hearing loss on that representation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spectral contrast threshold is higher for listeners with hearing loss than for listeners with normal hearing.
the spectral resolution of listeners with hearing loss is poorer than normal, and this poorer resolution contributes to their difficulties in speech perception in noise.
the spectral contrast threshold is higher for hearing-impaired listeners than for listeners with normal hearing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

listeners with hearing loss have difficulty with the perception of the spectral shape of complex sounds, which may have a significant effect on their ability to understand speech sounds in background noise.

listeners with sensorineural hearing impairment show an increase in spectral contrast threshold, and this increase appears to be due to the loss of cochlear frequency resolution, reduced cochlear gain, and altered cochlear phase characteristics in damaged areas of the cochlea.

hearing loss results in a reduction in spectral resolution that affects the discrimination of complex stimuli with a single spectral component, and this reduction in resolution is not compensated by the auditory system in the same manner as it is for normal listeners.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the spectral contrast thresholds of the listeners with normal hearing were similar to the absolute thresholds of the listeners who had hearing impairment, and the spectral contrast thresholds were similar in magnitude to those reported for normal-hearing listeners in other studies.
the ability of listeners to discriminate spectral shape is reduced in listeners with hearing impairment.
hearing-impaired listeners are impaired in their ability to perceive the spectral shape of complex sounds.
